hook.text: A user uploads a photo. Instantly, it's resized, tagged by AI, and stored — all without a running server.

buildup.text: Event-driven architecture connects services through events: something happens, something reacts.

discovery.text: Each event triggers a function or service. No polling, no waiting. Actions happen in real time.

twist.text: Debugging event-driven systems is brutal. When things break, tracing which event caused which failure is hard.

climax.text: Event-driven design powers modern apps at massive scale: Uber, Netflix, Airbnb all rely on it.

punchline.text: Events connect everything. Following the chain is the hard part.

quiz.question: What is the main challenge of event-driven architecture?
options: Debugging and tracing the chain of events when failures occur
Events can only trigger one service at a time
Event-driven systems cannot handle more than 100 users

details.summary: Event-driven architecture uses events like file uploads, database changes, or messages to trigger processing automatically. Cloud services like EventBridge, Pub/Sub, and Event Grid route events between producers and consumers without tight coupling.
details.whyItMatters: Event-driven design enables loosely coupled systems that scale independently and respond to changes in real time. It is the natural architecture for serverless and microservices.
takeaways: Events trigger processing without direct service coupling
Cloud event buses route events between services automatically

faq.question: What is an event in cloud computing?
faq.answer: An event is a notification that something happened: a file was uploaded, a database record changed, a user signed up, or a timer fired. Events carry enough information for consumers to react without querying the source system directly.

faq.question: What are the challenges of event-driven architecture?
faq.answer: Debugging distributed event flows is harder than tracing synchronous calls. Out-of-order events, duplicate delivery, and eventual consistency require careful design. Observability tooling that traces events across services is essential for production reliability.
